item.question: Two rubber bands of 4 cm cross at right angles at their midpoints. Name the quadrilateral their ends make, and name it again after one band is extended by 2 cm at each end.
steps_tex: The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so the quadrilateral is a rectangle.
They also meet at $90^\circ$, so all four sides are equal: it is a square.
The extended band is now $2 + 4 + 2 = 8\text{ cm}$ long and still has its midpoint at the crossing.
The diagonals still bisect each other at $90^\circ$, so all four sides are equal, but the diagonals are $4\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$, so it is not a rectangle.
item.answer_tex: First a square; after extending one diagonal, a rhombus

The diagonals still bisect each other at 90°, so all four sides are equal, but the diagonals are 4 cm and 8 cm, so it is not a rectangle.
item.answer: First a square; after extending one diagonal, a rhombus

item.question: ABCD is a kite with AB = BC and CD = DA, and its diagonals meet at O. Show that BD bisects ∠ABC and that BD is perpendicular to AC with AO = OC.
steps_tex: In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$: $AB = CB$, $AD = CD$, and $BD$ is common, so $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD$ by $SSS$.
So $\angle ABD = \angle CBD$: $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ (and likewise $\angle ADC$).
In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COB$: $AB = CB$, $\angle ABO = \angle CBO$, and $BO$ is common, so $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COB$ by $SAS$.
So $AO = OC$, and $\angle AOB = \angle COB$.
These two angles make a straight angle of $180$, so each is $180 \div 2 = 90$.
item.answer_tex: $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$, and it cuts $AC$ in half at right angles
steps: In ∆ABD and ∆CBD: AB = CB, AD = CD, and BD is common, so ∆ABD ≅ ∆CBD by SSS.
So ∠ABD = ∠CBD: BD bisects ∠ABC (and likewise ∠ADC).
In ∆AOB and ∆COB: AB = CB, ∠ABO = ∠CBO, and BO is common, so ∆AOB ≅ ∆COB by SAS.
So AO = OC, and ∠AOB = ∠COB.
These two angles make a straight angle of 180, so each is 180 ÷ 2 = 90.
item.answer: BD bisects ∠ABC and ∠ADC, and it cuts AC in half at right angles
item.text:
$1$. In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$: $AB = CB$, $AD = CD$, and $BD$ is common, so $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD$ by $SSS$.
$2$. So $\angle ABD = \angle CBD$: $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ (and likewise $\angle ADC$).
$3$. In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COB$: $AB = CB$, $\angle ABO = \angle CBO$, and $BO$ is common, so $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COB$ by $SAS$.
$4$. So $AO = OC$, and $\angle AOB = \angle COB$.
$5$. These two angles make a straight angle of $180$, so each is $180 \div 2 = 90$.
Answer: $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$, and it cuts $AC$ in half at right angles

item.question: Construct a kite whose diagonals are of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm.
steps_tex: Draw $AC = 6\text{ cm}$ and draw its perpendicular bisector, meeting $AC$ at $O$.
On the bisector mark $B$ at $2\text{ cm}$ from $O$ on one side and $D$ at $6\text{ cm}$ from $O$ on the other side, so $BD = 2 + 6 = 8\text{ cm}$.
Join $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ in order.
$B$ and $D$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, so $BA = BC$ and $DA = DC$: $ABCD$ is a kite.
Splitting $8\text{ cm}$ as $4\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$ would give a rhombus, which is a special kite.

item.question: Trapezium PQRS has PQ || SR, ∠P = 70° and ∠Q = 55°. Find ∠S and ∠R.
steps: PS is a transversal to the parallel lines PQ and SR, so ∠S + ∠P = 180.
QR is a transversal too, so ∠R = 180 − 55 = 125.
item.text:
Worked example: Trapezium PQRS has PQ || SR, ∠P = 70° and ∠Q = 55°. Find ∠S and ∠R.
1. PS is a transversal to the parallel lines PQ and SR, so ∠S + ∠P = 180.
2. So ∠S = 180 − 70 = 110.
3. QR is a transversal too, so ∠R = 180 − 55 = 125.
4. Check: 70 + 55 + 125 + 110 = 360.
Answer: ∠S = 110° and ∠R = 125°

item.question: UVWX is an isosceles trapezium with UV || XW, UX = VW and ∠U = 65°. Find ∠V, ∠W and ∠X.
steps: Draw XY and WZ perpendicular to UV; XWZY is a rectangle, so XY = WZ.
∆UXY and ∆VWZ have right angles at Y and Z, UX = VW and XY = WZ, so ∆UXY ≅ ∆VWZ by RHS.
UX is a transversal to the parallel sides, so ∠X = 180 − 65 = 115, and likewise ∠W = 115.
item.text:
Worked example: UVWX is an isosceles trapezium with UV || XW, UX = VW and ∠U = 65°. Find ∠V, ∠W and ∠X.
1. Draw XY and WZ perpendicular to UV; XWZY is a rectangle, so XY = WZ.
2. ∆UXY and ∆VWZ have right angles at Y and Z, UX = VW and XY = WZ, so ∆UXY ≅ ∆VWZ by RHS.
3. So ∠V = ∠U = 65.
4. UX is a transversal to the parallel sides, so ∠X = 180 − 65 = 115, and likewise ∠W = 115.
Answer: ∠V = 65°, ∠W = 115°, ∠X = 115°

item.question: Find the remaining angles in the following trapeziums. (i) A trapezium with angles 105° and 135° at the ends of one parallel side. (ii) An isosceles trapezium with an angle of 100°.
steps_tex: (i): Each slanting side is a transversal to the parallel sides, so its two angles add up to $180$.

(ii): The slanting sides are equal, so the angles at the ends of the same parallel side are equal: the other one next to $100$ is also $100$.
The angles below them are $180 - 100 = 80$ each.

item.question: Give every family name that belongs to a square.
steps: All its angles are 90°, so it is a rectangle.
All its sides are equal, so it is a rhombus.
Its opposite sides are parallel, so it is a parallelogram, and so also a trapezium.
Its neighbouring sides are equal in two pairs, so it is a kite.
item.answer: A square is a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram, a trapezium and a kite

item.question: The diagonals AC and BD of ABCD bisect each other at O at right angles. Show that ABCD is a rhombus.
steps: OA = OC and OB = OD, because the diagonals bisect each other.
The four angles at O are each 90.
In ∆AOB and ∆COB: OA = OC, ∠AOB = ∠COB, and OB is common, so they are congruent by SAS and AB = CB.
In the same way BC = CD and CD = DA.
All four sides are equal, so ABCD is a rhombus.

item.question: Draw a Venn diagram showing the set of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles, and squares. Then, answer the following questions. (i) What is the quadrilateral that is both a kite and a parallelogram? (ii) Can there be a quadrilateral that is both a kite and a rectangle? (iii) Is every kite a rhombus? If not, what is the correct relationship between these two types of quadrilaterals?
steps: Draw parallelograms holding rectangles and rhombuses, with squares in their overlap; draw kites overlapping parallelograms exactly in the rhombuses.
(i) A parallelogram has opposite sides equal; a kite has neighbouring sides equal in pairs, so all four sides are equal: a rhombus (squares included).
(ii) A kite that is a rectangle has equal neighbouring sides and opposite sides equal, so all sides are equal and all angles 90°: a square.
(iii) No. A kite can have sides 6, 6, 9 and 9, which is not a rhombus. Every rhombus is a kite.
item.answer: (i) A rhombus; (ii) Yes, a square; (iii) No; every rhombus is a kite, but not every kite is a rhombus

item.question: If a quadrilateral has four equal sides and one angle of 90°, will it be a square? Find the answer using geometric reasoning as well as by construction and measurement.
steps_tex: Four equal sides make it a rhombus, so it is a parallelogram.
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to $180$, so the neighbours of $90$ are $180 - 90 = 90$.
The opposite angle equals $90$ too, so all four angles are $90$.
Four equal sides and four right angles make a square.
steps: Four equal sides make it a rhombus, so it is a parallelogram.

The opposite angle equals 90 too, so all four angles are 90.
Four equal sides and four right angles make a square.

$4$. Four equal sides and four right angles make a square.
Answer: Yes, it is a square

item.question: State whether the following statements are true or false. Justify your answers. (i) A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square. (ii) A quadrilateral having three right angles must be a rectangle. (iii) A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other must be a parallelogram. (iv) A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus. (v) A quadrilateral in which the opposite angles are equal must be a parallelogram. (vi) A quadrilateral in which all the angles are equal is a rectangle. (vii) Isosceles trapeziums are parallelograms.
steps_tex: (i): False: such diagonals give a rectangle, which need not be a square.
(ii): True: the fourth angle is $360 - 270 = 90$.
(iii): True: the triangles at the crossing are congruent in opposite pairs, giving equal alternate angles, so opposite sides are parallel.
(iv): False: a kite has perpendicular diagonals but need not be a rhombus.
(v): True: with angles $x$, $y$, $x$, $y$ we get $2x + 2y = 360$, so neighbouring angles add up to $180$ and opposite sides are parallel.
(vi): True: each angle is $360 \div 4 = 90$.
(vii): False: its slanting sides are not parallel, unless it is a rectangle.

item.question: A sheet is folded in half and then into a quarter, and one slanting crease is made across the corner at the middle of the sheet. What shape do the creases make, and how should you fold to get a square?
steps: The two folds cross at right angles at the centre of the sheet.
Unfolding copies the crease into all four quarters, so the shape has four equal sides.
Its diagonals lie along the folds, so they bisect each other at right angles: a rhombus.
Several creases parallel to the first give rhombuses inside one another.
If the crease cuts off equal lengths along both folds, the diagonals are equal too, and the rhombus is a square.
item.answer: A rhombus; fold the crease at 45°, cutting equal lengths on both folds, to get a square

4. Several creases parallel to the first give rhombuses inside one another.
5. If the crease cuts off equal lengths along both folds, the diagonals are equal too, and the rhombus is a square.
